record.original_question: What is the minimum number of colours needed for every Earth–Moon map, where each country and its colony receive the same colour and adjacent countries or colonies receive different colours?

evidence.quote: Question 7.3 What is the minimum number of colours necessary to colour all Earth–Moon maps?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An Earth–Moon map consists of a finite collection of countries, where each country comprises exactly two regions: one region drawn on a sphere representing the Earth and one region drawn on a separate sphere representing the Moon. Each individual region (on either sphere) is a connected, simply connected closed subset, and on each sphere the regions form a planar map (their interiors are pairwise disjoint and any two regions meet, if at all, along boundary arcs). Two countries are said to be adjacent if some region of one shares a boundary arc with some region of the other (on either the Earth or the Moon). A proper colouring of an Earth–Moon map is an assignment of a colour to each country (so that the Earth region and Moon region of the same country receive the same colour) such that any two adjacent countries receive different colours.

Equivalently, in graph-theoretic terms, associate to each Earth–Moon map the graph G whose vertices are the countries and whose edges correspond to adjacencies; such a graph G is precisely a biplanar graph, i.e., a graph that can be written as the edge-union of two planar graphs on the same vertex set.

Determine the smallest integer k such that every Earth–Moon map admits a proper colouring using at most k colours; equivalently, determine
   max { χ(G) : G is biplanar }.
artifact.status_search_result: The Earth–Moon (biplanar) chromatic number is known to lie between 9 and 12: Heawood-style arguments give the upper bound 12, and a 9-chromatic biplanar graph (e.g., the join of C5 and K6) is known. No biplanar graph requiring 10, 11, or 12 colours has been exhibited, and the exact value remains unknown. Gethner (2018) conjectured the answer is 11. The problem is listed as open in standard references including the Open Problem Garden and Wikipedia.
